newsitem.title: UK: BoE's Davies - EMU holds dangers for the unprepared.
newsitem.headline: BoE's Davies - EMU holds dangers for the unprepared.

text.p: Bank of England deputy governor Howard Davies said on Monday that European Economic and Monetary Union offered many advantages but held real dangers for countries that were not sufficiently prepared.

Davies told a European Financial Management and Marketing Association conference in Brussels that for European countries which had not enjoyed a long history of moderate inflation and sound finances, the EMU mission was fraught with danger.
The text of his remarks was issued in London.

"We are convinced that if a single currency is to be a success, then all participants must be satisfied that they can survive within the EMU disciplines in the long-term, as well as the short," Davies said.
For that reason, he said it would be foolish for countries to massage down public deficits in 1997, just to meet the 1998 deadline when the decision will be taken on which countries qualify for EMU.
"It would be unwise because the deficit limit is not a one-off requirement."
Davies said Friday's agreement on a stability pact at the European Union summit in Dublin laid out the disciplines necessary to keep participating nations' finances in order.

"Member states will need to live with continued fiscal discipline," he said. "Unless a country can show that in mid-cycle, with the economy growing at trend...the budget of the government would tend to be close to balance, then it may find the fiscal discipline of EMU difficult."
For Britain, he noted the budget deficit remains above the Maastricht Treaty guideline of three percent of GDP despite five years of economic growth.
"A UK government of any political colour...will be bound to take that into consideration." He also noted the dangers of rigidity in the European labour market.

He said only the UK, of possible EMU participants, could point to shifts in relative unemployment rates from richer to poorer areas in recent years. That was due to the dismantling of various labour market restrictions in the 1980s.

"Elsewhere in Europe, those changes have not been made. Without them, we would have to enter a reserve on the preparedness of some European economies for the rigours of a single currency," Davies said.
He said labour market reforms should be undertaken before the euro is born.
Whether Britain enters EMU or not, Davies stressed that its success was strongly in Britain's interests.
He added that London would retain its pre-eminence as Europe's number one financial centre either way.
"We are confident that London will be as well prepared for EMU as any market, when the time comes."
